faqs.q: Why do raccoons keep getting into Troy homes?
faqs.a: Our crew's Troy work centers on Norway rats and pigeons downtown, raccoons and squirrels on the hillside streets, and bats in the big older homes. The pattern follows the housing and the habitat: hudson river keeps animals close, and once one finds a way into a roofline, chimney, or crawlspace here, it usually comes back until every entry is sealed. That is why we pair removal with proofing on every Troy job rather than just taking the animal out.

Troy.wildlife_intro:
Troy keeps our crew busy with Norway rats and pigeons downtown, raccoons and squirrels on the hillside streets, and bats in the big older homes. Hudson River  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Troy. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Troy jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Rensselaer?
faqs.a: Hillside lots and older attached housing make Rensselaer inspections wider than a flat suburban job — retaining-wall voids, cellar entries, and stacked rooflines all get checked before a figure is honest. Once we have walked the property we give you a written quote that covers removal and sealing as a single scope.

faqs.q: Why do rats get worse in Rensselaer when the Hudson runs high?
faqs.a: High water floods the burrows and low sewer runs along the riverfront, and Norway rats move uphill into basements and foundation gaps until the water drops. Sealing foundation penetrations and floor-drain gaps before flood season is the durable answer; our crew maps those below-grade entries during the inspection and closes them as part of the job.

Rensselaer.wildlife_intro:
Rensselaer sits on the Hudson's east bank looking straight across at Albany, and its oldest streets climb the hill behind the Amtrak station in tight, pre-war rows. Norway rats are the steady call in the riverfront blocks and older commercial cellars, raccoons work the chimneys on the hill streets, and squirrels move through the canopy in the upper neighborhoods. Fort Crailo's colonial blocks at the south end add some of the oldest housing in the county.

The hill shapes the work here: roofs stack above roofs, and animals traveling the tree line cross several properties in a night. Fall sends squirrels into the hill-street attics, spring puts raccoon families in flues, and the riverfront sees rat activity spike whenever high water pushes them out of low ground. Our crew inspects Rensselaer homes from cellar to chimney cap, removes the animals, and seals both the roofline and the below-grade openings that a river city produces.

faqs.q: What does wildlife removal cost in East Greenbush?
faqs.a: A straightforward squirrel entry on a 1960s ranch is a small job; a groundhog system under a deck plus a raccoon in the chimney is not, and the only way to know which you have is to look. We inspect the attic, roofline, and ground-level voids, then quote the whole removal-and-screening scope in writing.

faqs.q: What is digging under my East Greenbush deck?
faqs.a: On East Greenbush's open suburban lots it is usually a groundhog, with skunks a close second — both favor the sheltered, undisturbed space under decks and shed floors. Our crew confirms which animal from the burrow size and tracks, removes it, and installs screening around the structure so the void does not simply refill next season.

East Greenbush.wildlife_intro:
East Greenbush is the suburban hill town directly east of the Hudson crossings, built out along Columbia Turnpike with a mix of 1960s subdivisions, newer developments, and surviving farm parcels. Gray squirrels are the everyday attic call in the mature subdivisions, groundhogs work the open back lots and garden edges, and raccoons den in chimneys across the older streets near the Rensselaer line. Wooded ravines cutting through the town keep skunks and opossums in circulation year-round.

The newer the subdivision, the more the calls shift to ground level: groundhog burrows under decks and sheds, skunks under front porches, moles in irrigated lawns. Older sections see the classic pattern instead — fall squirrel entries, spring raccoon litters. Our crew inspects East Greenbush homes inside and out, removes the animals, and screens the ground-level voids that suburban lots here offer in abundance, not just the roofline.

faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Brunswick?
faqs.a: Brunswick properties often include a barn, shed, or garage alongside the house, and whether those structures are part of the job changes the scope more than the animal does. We inspect what you ask us to cover, explain the options plainly, and quote removal and sealing in writing before starting.

faqs.q: Do Brunswick farms get different wildlife problems than the suburbs?
faqs.a: Yes — feed storage, livestock, and open burrowing ground make farm properties a draw for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs in a way a subdivision lot is not, while the farmhouse itself still gets the usual bats and squirrels. Our crew separates the two problems at inspection: proofing the house, and screening the outbuildings where the yard animals den.

Brunswick.wildlife_intro:
Brunswick wraps around Troy's eastern side in a patchwork of suburban streets, working farms, and wooded creek valleys, and its calls split the same way. Near the Troy line, squirrels and raccoons fill older attics; out along the farm roads, groundhogs burrow fence lines and barn foundations, skunks den under outbuildings, and opossums work the compost-and-livestock edges of small farms. The Poestenkill valley adds a wooded corridor that moves animals between properties.

Brunswick's long, cold winters push everything toward buildings early: bats settle into farmhouse eaves by late summer, squirrels claim suburban attics in October, and spring thaw brings groundhogs out along every sunny bank. Our crew treats Brunswick properties whole — house, barn, and shed in one inspection — removes the animals, and seals the dwelling first, then screens the outbuilding voids that keep restocking the yard.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Schodack?
faqs.a: Older Schodack farmhouses usually carry more entry points than newer construction — settled sills, layered additions, and open eaves — so the inspection, not the animal, sets the price. We walk the house and any outbuildings in scope, show you each opening, and give you a written quote for removal and sealing.

faqs.q: I found bats in my Schodack farmhouse. What happens next?
faqs.a: Bat work is exclusion, not trapping: our crew identifies the entry points, installs one-way exits, and seals the rest, scheduling the work around the maternity season as professional practice so flightless young are not trapped inside. Bats are a designated rabies-vector species in New York, so a bat found in living space is handled under health-department guidance — never barehanded.

Schodack.wildlife_intro:
Schodack fronts the Hudson south of Albany with Schodack Island's river forest on one side and farm country rolling east on the other, and its housing is mostly older farmhouses, hamlet streets in Castleton, and scattered subdivisions. Big brown bats are a signature call in the big old farmhouses, raccoons work the river-edge woods into attics and barns, and groundhogs and skunks cover the open ground in between. Castleton's compact village adds squirrels and the occasional rat complaint near its older commercial core.

River fog and long winters make Schodack's older homes attractive winter roosts: a bat colony can pass a whole season in a farmhouse wall void unnoticed. Spring brings raccoon mothers into barns and chimneys, and summer groundhog digging peaks along the field edges. Our crew inspects Schodack homes with the outbuildings included, removes the animals, and seals the house envelope — eave gaps on a two-century-old farmhouse take a different plan than a subdivision soffit, and we quote it that way.
